theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: Describe the steps of the communication process, from the sender to the feedback, and give an example from a workplace.
essays.modelAnswer: Communication starts with a sender who has an idea or information to share. The sender puts the idea into words, pictures or signs that the other person will understand. Next the sender chooses a channel, the way the message travels, such as speaking face to face, a phone call, a text, a memo or a notice. The receiver gets the message and works out what it means. Finally the receiver gives feedback, a reply or an action that shows the sender how the message was understood. If the feedback shows a mistake, the sender explains again. For example, a supervisor tells a trainee, Kemar, to switch off and unplug the grinder before changing the disc. Kemar repeats the instruction back, and the supervisor knows the message was understood.
markingPoints: Sender has an idea or information and puts it into words or signs
A channel is chosen (spoken, phone, written, notice)
Receiver gets the message and works out its meaning
Feedback shows how it was understood; sender corrects any mistake
A suitable workplace example

essays.stem: Explain how you would listen actively when your supervisor gives you instructions for a new job.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would stop what I am doing, put away my phone and face the supervisor so that I can give full attention. If the area is noisy, I would ask to move somewhere quieter or wait until the machine is off. While the supervisor speaks I would keep eye contact, nod and not cut in. I would write short notes of the key points, such as the job, the materials, the time it must be finished and any safety rules. When the supervisor finishes, I would ask questions about anything I am not sure of. Then I would repeat the main points back in my own words so that the supervisor can check that I have understood correctly before I start the job.
markingPoints: Stops other work and gives full attention (faces speaker, no phone)
Deals with noise or distractions
Shows listening: eye contact, nodding, not interrupting
Takes short notes of key points
Asks questions and repeats back (paraphrases) to check understanding

essays.stem: Describe three barriers to communication at work and say how each one can be overcome.
essays.modelAnswer: One barrier is noise. In a workshop, a salon with dryers running or a busy hotel kitchen, people may not hear a message. This can be overcome by moving to a quieter place, waiting until a machine is switched off, or using agreed hand signals. A second barrier is language. A customer or co-worker may speak another language, or the speaker may use trade jargon that the listener does not know. This can be overcome by using short, plain words, explaining trade terms, showing a picture or a demonstration, and checking understanding. A third barrier is emotion. A person who is angry, worried or tired may not listen well. This can be overcome by staying calm, choosing a better time to talk and letting the person explain before you reply.
markingPoints: First barrier named with a way to overcome it
Second barrier named with a way to overcome it
Third barrier named with a way to overcome it
Examples are realistic for a workplace
Says to check understanding

essays.stem: Describe the steps for taking a telephone message for a co-worker who is not there.
essays.modelAnswer: I would answer the phone politely within a few rings, greet the caller and give the business name and my name. I would explain that the person they want is not available and offer to take a message. I would have a message pad or form and a pen ready. I would write down the caller's full name, the company if there is one, the phone number, the message, and whether the caller wants a call back. I would ask the caller to spell any name I am not sure of. Before the call ends, I would read the details back to check them. I would write the date and time of the call and my own name on the message, thank the caller, and then give the message to the co-worker or put it where they will see it straight away.
markingPoints: Answers politely, giving business name and own name
Has a pen and message pad or form ready
Records caller's name, number, message and if a call back is wanted
Reads the message back to check it
Adds date, time and own name and passes the message on quickly

essays.stem: Describe what a memo should contain and how it should be set out. Use the example of a memo telling staff about a change to working hours.
essays.modelAnswer: A memo is a short written message used inside a business. It begins with a heading block: To (all staff), From (the name and job of the writer, for example Mrs Campbell, Manager), Date, and Subject (Change to working hours from Monday 3 November). The body should be short and clear. The first sentence gives the main point: from Monday the workshop and salon will open at 7:30 a.m. and close at 4:00 p.m. The next sentences give the reason, for example to avoid the afternoon heat, and anything staff must do, such as check the new shift list on the notice board. It ends with who to contact with questions. The writer uses plain words, checks spelling, dates and times, and may sign or initial it.
markingPoints: Heading: To, From, Date, Subject
Main point stated first, clearly
Gives reason and any action staff must take
Plain, short language with correct dates and times
Says who to contact and is checked before sending

essays.stem: Explain why body language matters when you deal with customers, and give examples of good and poor body language.
essays.modelAnswer: Body language is the message we give with our face, eyes, hands and the way we stand. Customers often notice it before they hear our words, and they believe it more than words. If our body language is poor, a customer may feel unwelcome or think we do not care, even if we say the right things. Good body language includes a smile, good eye contact, an open posture with arms relaxed, facing the customer and nodding while they speak. Poor body language includes folded arms, frowning, looking at a phone, yawning, turning away or standing too close. For example, a guest arriving at a villa feels welcome when the attendant stands up, smiles and makes eye contact. Good body language builds trust and helps keep customers coming back.
markingPoints: Explains what body language is
Says customers notice and believe it, so it affects how they feel
Gives at least two examples of good body language
Gives at least two examples of poor body language
Links good body language to trust or repeat business

essays.stem: A customer complains to you face to face that their job was not finished on time. Describe how you would communicate with the customer to deal with the complaint.
essays.modelAnswer: I would stay calm and polite and give the customer my full attention. I would let them explain the whole problem without cutting in, and I would show that I am listening by nodding and keeping eye contact. When they finish, I would say that I understand why they are upset and thank them for telling me. I would not argue or blame a co-worker. I would ask questions to get the facts, such as the job number and the date it was promised, and write them down. If I can fix the problem, I would explain clearly what will be done and when. If I cannot, I would tell the customer that I will pass it to my supervisor and say when they will hear back. Then I would make sure the supervisor gets the details and follow up.
markingPoints: Stays calm, polite and listens without interrupting
Shows understanding; does not argue or blame others
Asks questions and writes down the facts
Explains clearly what will happen and when
Refers to the supervisor if needed and follows up

essays.stem: Explain how a worker should take part in a work meeting before, during and after it.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the meeting, the worker should read the agenda, think about the topics, and prepare any facts or questions, such as a list of tools that need replacing. They should arrive on time with a pen and notebook. During the meeting, they should switch the phone to silent, listen when others speak, and wait for their turn. When they speak, they should be clear, polite and keep to the topic. They should respect other views even when they disagree, and ask questions if something is not clear. They should note any decisions and any task given to them. After the meeting, they should read the minutes, carry out their tasks by the agreed date, and tell the person in charge when each task is done or if there is a problem.
markingPoints: Before: reads agenda and prepares, arrives on time
During: listens, takes turns, keeps to the topic
Respects other views and asks questions
Notes decisions and own tasks
After: reads minutes, does tasks on time and reports back

essays.stem: Explain why workers must read and follow written instructions, labels and safety signs. Give examples from at least two different trades.
essays.modelAnswer: Written instructions, labels and signs tell workers how to do a job safely and correctly. They give facts that a person may not remember, and they are the same for everyone, so less is left to guessing. If a worker does not read them, they may be hurt, hurt someone else, damage tools or materials, or waste a customer's money. For example, in a salon the label on a hair colour or chemical gives the mixing amounts, the time to leave it on, and first-aid steps if it gets in the eyes. In electrical work the instructions for a new appliance give the correct rating and how to connect it. In a welding shop a warning sign shows where hot work is happening, and a mandatory sign shows that eye protection must be worn. Workers should ask if anything is unclear.
markingPoints: Instructions, labels and signs give the safe and correct method
Not reading them can cause injury, damage or waste
Example from one trade
Example from a second trade
Ask if anything is unclear; follow the maker's instructions

essays.stem: Compare spoken and written communication at work. Give two advantages of each, and say when you would use each one.
essays.modelAnswer: Spoken communication is fast. A message can be given at once, and the listener can ask questions and get answers straight away, so it is easier to check understanding. Tone of voice and body language also help to show meaning. Written communication gives a lasting record that can be checked later, and the same message can reach many people in the same words. It is also useful when details such as numbers, measurements or dates must be exact. I would use spoken communication for quick instructions, a warning in an emergency, or talking through a problem with a co-worker. I would use written communication for job cards, incident reports, orders, a change of rules for all staff, or a message for someone who is not there. Often both are used: speak first, then confirm in writing.
markingPoints: Two advantages of spoken communication
Two advantages of written communication
When spoken is the better choice, with an example
When written is the better choice, with an example
Notes that both can be used together

practical1.title: Telephone calls and message slips: a group role play
practical1.brief: As a group, act out a set of work phone calls and record each one on a message slip. The assessor gives each member a different scenario card: for example a customer asking for a gate to be welded, a client booking a salon appointment, a householder reporting a faulty socket, or a guest asking about a villa booking. Each member plays the caller once and the person answering once. The person answering greets the caller properly, takes the message on a slip, reads it back, and then passes it on by speaking to the member who plays the co-worker. The other members watch and fill in a short feedback sheet for each call. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the completed message slips and feedback sheets once for the whole group.
materials: Scenario cards (one per member, from the assessor)
Blank telephone message slips (at least 2 per member)
Two phones, or two practice handsets
photos: The group with the scenario cards and blank message slips set out
Each member answering a call (one photo per member)
Each completed message slip, clear enough to read
A member passing a message on to the co-worker
The completed feedback sheets laid out together
checklist: Answered politely, giving the business name and own name
Listened without interrupting and asked suitable questions
Wrote the caller's name, number, message, date and time on the slip
Read the message back to the caller to check it
Passed the message on clearly and correctly to the co-worker
Spoke clearly as a caller and stayed in role
Gave fair, polite feedback to another member
safety: Keep phone and charger cables out of walkways so no one trips
Sit or stand where the group is not in the way of others or a fire exit
Use only made-up names and numbers; do not record real customers' details

practical2.title: Write a staff notice and give a short briefing on it
practical2.brief: As a group, write a one-page notice for staff about a workplace rule, and then brief the rest of the class on it. The assessor gives the topic, for example "Clean your work area and put tools away before you leave" or "How to report an accident". First, plan together what the notice must say. Each member writes one part in rough: the heading, the main point, the reasons, what staff must do, and who to contact. Then the group checks the draft for plain words, spelling and correct facts, and marks the corrections. Make the final notice neat and easy to read from 2 metres, using one or two simple pictures or signs. Finally, each member presents one part of the notice in a short briefing of about 5 minutes and answers one question from the audience. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Chart paper or a large sheet for the final notice
A dictionary, on paper or on a phone
photos: The group planning the notice, with the plan visible
The rough draft showing each member's part and the corrections
The finished notice, clear enough to read
Each member presenting their part (one photo per member)
The notes of the questions asked and the answers given
checklist: Took part in planning and wrote their own part of the draft
Used short sentences and plain words
Found and corrected at least one mistake in spelling, grammar or facts
Spoke clearly, faced the audience and kept to the point
Used suitable body language: eye contact and an open posture
Listened to a question and answered it politely and correctly
Respected other members' ideas during the group work
safety: Use markers in a ventilated room and put the caps back on
Keep bags and chart paper off the floor in walkways
Use scissors or a craft knife, if needed, with care and put them away after use
